hibák:

	1.	RSF lifetime management is racy: deinit writes self.ctrl = null before taking c.mutex, while withCtrlLocked and isGPUAvailable read self.ctrl before any lock is held. A concurrent caller can therefore read a stale ControlBlock*, then deinit can free that control block, and the caller can proceed to lock or read freed memory.
	2.	The GPU state cannot represent the full model when num_layers > 1. syncAllLayersGPU loops over all layers, but accel.RSFAccelerator.init(dim) receives no layer count, and setWeightsS / setWeightsT receive no layer index. Each iteration therefore overwrites the same accelerator-side parameters, so the GPU path cannot faithfully encode a stacked RSF.
	3.	The GPU sync code uploads only s_weight and t_weight. It never uploads s_bias, t_bias, clip_min, or clip_max, even though the CPU path uses all of them in computeScale and computeTranslation. As soon as biases are nonzero, or any per-layer clip settings matter, GPU forward can diverge from CPU forward.
	4.	GPU failures are silently swallowed instead of invalidating the GPU path. In RSF.forward, both ga.forwardFromTensor(...) errors and wrong-shaped GPU results are ignored, gpu_available stays true, and the code just falls back to CPU. That means a broken GPU path is retried forever and its failures are hidden.
	5.	The GPU forward path skips the numeric validation that the CPU path relies on. The CPU implementation checks for non-finite values after the layer transforms; the GPU branch copies the GPU result straight into x if the shape matches, with no NaN/Inf check. That makes CPU and GPU behavior observably inconsistent on bad numerics.
	6.	RSF.save has a double-close bug. The file handle is protected by errdefer { file.close(); ... }, but file.close() is also called explicitly before rename. If rename(tmp_name, path) fails, the errdefer runs and closes the already-closed file handle again.
	7.	The file checksum does not cover all serialized fields. save writes max_dim and max_layers, but the CRC only hashes global clip values / grad_mean, per-layer clip values / grad_mean, and raw tensor data. A corruption in saved max_dim or max_layers is therefore not detected by the checksum, and with policy == null those corrupted values can silently change the loaded configuration.
	8.	RSF.backward is not exception-safe while building its gradient snapshot. It calls layer.ensureGradients() before all of the fallible allocator.dupe(...) snapshot operations have succeeded. If one of those allocations fails partway through, the function returns with some layers permanently mutated from “no gradient tensors allocated” to “gradient tensors allocated”.
	9.	The backward rollback restores only gradient contents, not original gradient existence. Even in the path where saved_grads is used to roll back after a later backward failure, layers that originally had null gradient tensors remain changed to allocated gradient tensors, because the code never records or restores the original null vs allocated state.
		1.	RSF is copyable by value even though it owns ctrl; copying it creates multiple owners of the same ControlBlock. Deinitializing one copy frees the block and leaves every other copy with a dangling pointer, so later method calls on those copies can dereference freed memory.
	2.	RSFLayer is also copyable by value even though it owns Tensor allocations and optional gradient tensors. Copying a layer duplicates ownership of the same allocations, so deinitializing both copies can double-free the same buffers.
	3.	withCtrlLocked() has a use-after-free race with deinit(): it reads self.ctrl before locking c.mutex. Another thread can null out self.ctrl, free c, and then the first thread will lock and use a freed mutex/control block.
	4.	isGPUAvailable() has the same race as withCtrlLocked(): it reads self.ctrl, then locks c.mutex. If another thread deinitializes and frees the control block in between, isGPUAvailable() can lock/use freed memory.
	5.	save() has a double-close bug on the error path after the explicit file.close(). If std.fs.cwd().rename(tmp_name, path) fails, the active errdefer runs and calls file.close() again on an already-closed handle.
	6.	GPU synchronization is incomplete: syncLayerGPU() uploads only s_weight and t_weight, but CPU forward/inverse also depend on s_bias, t_bias, clip_min, and clip_max. The GPU path therefore cannot reproduce CPU semantics once biases are nonzero or clip values differ.
	7.	forward() may use the GPU path, but backward() always recomputes activations with forwardOnCPU(). If GPU math differs from CPU math at all, gradients are computed for a different forward pass than the one that actually produced the caller’s output.
	8.	inverse() is CPU-only while forward() may run on GPU. If the GPU path is not exactly identical to the CPU path, inverse(forward(x)) is no longer guaranteed to reconstruct x.
	9.	syncLayerGPU() casts weights to f16 with @floatCast without any range or finiteness validation. Large or non-finite weights can silently become inf/nan on the GPU side and corrupt inference.
	10.	loadWithConfig() validates shapes and config scalars but never validates that loaded tensor contents are finite. A checkpoint containing nan/inf weights or biases loads successfully and leaves the model in an invalid numeric state.
	11.	RSF.forward()’s GPU path copies the accelerator result directly into x without the CPU path’s non-finite checks. The same model can therefore reject nan/inf outputs on CPU but return them silently on GPU.
	12.	RSF.forward() silently swallows every accelerator error (else |_| {}) and every malformed GPU result that fails the shape check, then falls back to CPU without clearing gpu_available. Persistent GPU faults remain hidden and are retried indefinitely.
	13.	RSF.backward()’s rollback is not strong-exception-safe. It only restores gradient values after failures inside the per-layer backward loop; failures earlier in setup (for example in ensureGradients() or while duplicating saved gradients) can still mutate object state before returning an error.
	14.	Even on the rollback path, RSF.backward() restores only gradient contents, not the original null/non-null state of the optional gradient tensors. A failed backward can permanently change a lazily-uninitialized layer into one with allocated gradient tensors.
	15.	save() duplicates every parameter tensor into layer_data before writing. That doubles peak parameter memory during serialization and makes saving require O(model size) extra RAM instead of streaming directly to disk.
	16.	RSFLayer.forward(), inverse(), and backward() do repeated full-tensor copies/transposes of inputs and weights on every call (copy, transpose, extra temporaries). This creates substantial allocator churn and avoidable O(parameter + activation) copy overhead per layer.
	17.	RSF.backward() recomputes the full model forward pass on CPU from input, and then each RSFLayer.backward() reconstructs intermediate inputs again from outputs. That duplicates a large amount of work and makes backward materially more expensive than necessary.
	18.	The single ControlBlock mutex is held across entire CPU forward, inverse, backward, gradient-zeroing, and GPU-sync operations. That coarse lock serializes all work through one critical section and prevents scalable concurrent use of the same model.
	19.	save() uses "{path}.{timestamp}.tmp" with millisecond resolution for its temp filename. Two separate processes or two different RSF instances saving to the same target within the same millisecond can collide on the same temp file name.
	20.	The on-disk CRC does not cover several structural fields that are written before tensor data, including the header/version, num_layers, dim, tensor ranks/shapes, and saved max_dim/max_layers. Corruption in those fields is therefore not fully protected by the checksum.
	21.	syncWeightsToGPU() reports success even when no GPU is available, because syncAllLayersGPU() simply returns early when gpu_available == 0. Callers cannot distinguish “weights synced” from “nothing happened.”
	22.	There is no automatic invalidation/bump of cpu_weight_version for ordinary in-memory parameter changes. After parameters are modified, the GPU path can keep using stale synchronized weights because only loadWithConfig() updates the CPU/GPU version relationship.
	23.	save() syncs the temporary file but never syncs the parent directory after rename. On filesystems that require a directory fsync for durable rename, a crash after the rename can still lose the supposedly saved checkpoint.
